subject: Samhällskunskap
title: Sweden, the EU and the world
sourceSummary: What the EU is and how decisions are made in the union, how EU membership affects Sweden, the UN's tasks and bodies, international cooperation on peace, trade and the environment, and what globalisation means.

questions.opener: Think about what kind of organisation it is — military, judicial, or political and economic cooperation.
choices: A military alliance led by the USA
A political and economic partnership between European countries, where the member states make some decisions jointly
A UN body that works on human rights
An international court for war crimes
questions.explanation: The EU is a partnership between currently 27 European countries that have handed over some decision-making to shared institutions, above all regarding trade, the single market, the environment and agriculture. Sweden became a member in 1995 following a referendum in 1994. The military alliance that the USA belongs to is NATO, a different organisation, and the International Criminal Court (ICC) is likewise not part of the EU.

questions.prompt: Which of the EU's institutions is directly elected by citizens in the member states?
questions.opener: One of the institutions gets its mandate in a general election held every five years.
choices: The European Commission
The Council of Ministers (the Council)
The European Parliament
The Court of Justice of the EU
questions.explanation: Members of the European Parliament are elected directly by voters in the member states in EU elections held every five years; Sweden elects 21 members. The Commission proposes new EU laws and consists of one commissioner from each country, the Council of Ministers consists of ministers from the member states, and the Court of Justice interprets EU law — none of them is directly elected by voters. The Commission's proposals are decided jointly by the Parliament and the Council of Ministers.

questions.prompt: What does the EU's single market mean for Sweden?
questions.opener: Four things should be able to move freely across borders.
choices: Free movement of goods, services, capital and people between the member states
That Sweden must have the euro as its currency
That Swedish companies are not allowed to sell outside the EU
That all prices in EU countries are equally high
questions.explanation: The single market is built on the four freedoms: goods, services, capital and people should be able to move freely between the member states, which makes it easier to trade, study and work in other EU countries. Sweden kept the krona after the referendum on the euro in 2003, so a shared currency is not part of membership for Sweden. Companies can of course also trade with countries outside the EU, and prices still differ between countries.

questions.prompt: What is one of the UN's most important tasks?
questions.opener: The UN was founded in 1945 with a clear main purpose after the world war.
choices: To pass laws that apply directly in every country in the world
To manage the EU's shared budget
To try individuals for ordinary crimes in member states
To work for peace and security in the world, for human rights and for development
questions.explanation: The UN was founded in 1945 and its main tasks are to maintain peace and security, promote human rights, provide disaster relief and work for sustainable development, among other things through the global goals in Agenda 2030. The General Assembly is the forum where every member state has one vote each, and the Security Council can decide on sanctions and peacekeeping operations. The UN does not, however, make laws that apply directly in countries — conventions must be ratified by each state — and the UN does not try ordinary criminal cases.

questions.prompt: What is the Paris Agreement from 2015 an example of?
questions.opener: The agreement is about a problem that no single country can solve on its own.
choices: A trade agreement between the EU and the USA
International cooperation on the climate, where countries promise to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to limit global warming
A military defence pact in Europe
A UN convention on children's rights
questions.explanation: The Paris Agreement is a global climate agreement in which countries commit to reducing their emissions so that warming is kept well below two degrees, aiming for 1.5 degrees. It is a classic example of a cross-border problem that requires cooperation, since emissions in one country affect the whole world. The convention on children's rights is the Convention on the Rights of the Child from 1989, an entirely different agreement.

questions.opener: Think about trade, technology, travel and information that tie the world together.
choices: That all countries get the same political system
That the world's countries close their borders to trade
That countries, economies and people are tied closer together through trade, technology, transport, travel and information flows
That everyone in the world speaks the same language
questions.explanation: Globalisation means that distances effectively shrink: goods, capital, information, culture and people move across borders to an ever-greater extent. It is usually described in terms of both opportunities — cheaper goods, wider choice, exchange of knowledge, and reduced poverty in parts of the world — and problems, such as jobs relocating, economic crises spreading quickly, and emissions and working conditions in producing countries becoming hard to control. Globalisation is thus about interconnection, not about political systems or languages becoming the same.

questions.prompt: Give examples of three different ways that EU membership affects everyday life in Sweden, and explain why.
questions.opener: Think about travelling, shopping and living in a country with shared environmental rules.
questions.answer: A first example is the free movement of people: as an EU citizen you can travel, study and work in other member states without a work permit, and exchange programmes such as Erasmus make it easier to study abroad. Passport-free travel within the Schengen area also belongs here. A second example is trade and consumer rights: the single market means goods can be sold between EU countries without tariffs, which affects the range and prices in shops, and shared rules provide consumer protection — for example, abolished roaming charges so a mobile phone can be used at the same price across the whole EU, as well as shared requirements for product safety and ingredient lists. A third example is environment and climate: many of the rules that apply in Sweden on emissions, chemicals, waste and air quality are decided at EU level, and the EU's emissions trading system affects the price of electricity and industrial production. Behind all three examples lies the same mechanism: as a member, Sweden has handed over some decision-making to the EU, EU law takes precedence over national law within the areas the cooperation covers, and Sweden influences the decisions through its 21 members of the European Parliament and through the government's ministers in the Council of Ministers.
steps: Example 1 — free movement: the right to travel, study and work in other EU countries, plus passport-free travel within Schengen.
Example 2 — trade and consumer protection: no tariffs within the single market, shared product requirements and abolished roaming charges affect prices and rights.
Example 3 — environment and climate: many Swedish rules on emissions, chemicals and waste are decided at EU level, as is emissions trading.
Explain the mechanism: Sweden has handed over some decision-making to the EU, and EU law takes precedence within the areas the cooperation covers.
Point to Sweden's influence: 21 members of the European Parliament and Swedish ministers in the Council of Ministers take part in the decisions.

questions.prompt: Summarise the EU, the UN, international cooperation and globalisation, and how Sweden is affected.
questions.opener: From Brussels to New York — and the interconnection of the whole world.
questions.answer: The EU: political and economic partnership between 27 European countries · Sweden a member since 1995 after a referendum in 1994 · kept the krona after the euro referendum in 2003 · Institutions: the Commission proposes laws (one commissioner per country) · the European Parliament is directly elected by voters every five years (Sweden has 21 members) · the Council of Ministers consists of ministers from the member states · the European Council brings together heads of state and government · the Court of Justice interprets EU law · The single market: the four freedoms — free movement of goods, services, capital and people · affects Sweden through trade, working and studying abroad, consumer protection and environmental rules · The UN: founded in 1945 · works for peace and security, human rights, disaster relief and sustainable development (Agenda 2030) · the General Assembly = one vote per member state, the Security Council can decide on sanctions and peacekeeping operations · International cooperation: the Paris Agreement of 2015 on the climate, the WTO on trade rules, peacekeeping operations · needed because problems such as climate, pandemics and conflicts cross borders · Globalisation: countries and people are tied closer together through trade, technology, transport and information · opportunities (choice, exchange of knowledge, reduced poverty in parts of the world) and problems (jobs relocating, crises spreading quickly, emissions and working conditions hard to control).

questions.prompt: What is the EU's shared currency, used by most but not all member states?
questions.opener: Sweden has chosen not to adopt it.
choices: The dollar
The krona
The pound
The euro
questions.explanation: The euro is the EU's shared currency and is used by the majority of member states, but not all — Sweden, for example, has kept the Swedish krona. The dollar is the USA's currency and the pound the UK's, and the UK is, moreover, no longer an EU member.

questions.prompt: In which year did Sweden become an EU member?
questions.opener: Membership was preceded by a referendum the year before.
questions.explanation: Sweden became an EU member in 1995, after a referendum in 1994 in which a majority voted yes. In 2003, by contrast, the referendum on the euro was held, which resulted in a no, 1972 is before membership, and 1945 is the year the UN was founded.

questions.prompt: Which UN body can decide on sanctions and peacekeeping operations?
questions.opener: This body has a small number of permanent members with veto power.
choices: The General Assembly alone
The European Commission
NATO
The Security Council
questions.explanation: The Security Council is the UN body that can decide on binding sanctions and peacekeeping operations, with five permanent members holding veto power. The General Assembly can adopt resolutions but lacks the same binding power, and neither the European Commission nor NATO are UN bodies.

questions.prompt: What does the abbreviation WTO stand for, an organisation that works on international trade rules?
questions.opener: The last two letters reveal it's an organisation.
choices: The World Health Organization
The World Bank
The World Wide Fund for Nature
The World Trade Organization
questions.explanation: The WTO, the World Trade Organization, works on drawing up shared rules for international trade and resolving trade disputes between countries. The World Health Organization (WHO), the World Bank and the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) are other international organisations with entirely different main tasks.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is often mentioned as a possible disadvantage of globalisation?
questions.opener: Think about what can happen to jobs when production can easily move between countries.
choices: That trade between countries decreases entirely
That all countries become exactly equally wealthy
That the internet stops working
That jobs in certain industries relocate to countries with lower wages
questions.explanation: A commonly mentioned disadvantage of globalisation is that companies can move production and jobs to countries with lower wages, which can hit certain industries in high-income countries hard. Globalisation, on the contrary, means trade increases, it doesn't automatically equalise every country's wealth, and it has nothing to do with the internet ceasing to work.

questions.prompt: What is the agreement called that allows citizens to travel between most EU countries (and a few more) without passport checks at the borders?
questions.opener: The agreement is named after a small village in Luxembourg where it was signed.
choices: The Paris Agreement
The Treaty of Lisbon
The Treaty of Rome
The Schengen Agreement
questions.explanation: The Schengen Agreement allows citizens to travel between most EU countries and a few additional countries without passport checks at the internal borders. The Paris Agreement concerns the climate, and the Treaty of Lisbon and the Treaty of Rome are other foundational EU treaties, but neither of them regulates passport-free travel in the same way.

questions.prompt: Does Sweden use the euro or its own currency as an EU member?
questions.opener: The question was settled in a referendum in 2003.
choices: Sweden was forced to adopt the euro immediately upon membership
Sweden uses both the euro and the krona in parallel in every shop
Sweden has no currency of its own at all
Sweden has kept the Swedish krona
questions.explanation: Sweden has kept the Swedish krona as its currency, since a majority voted no to the euro in the 2003 referendum. Sweden was therefore not forced to adopt the euro upon membership, and the krona is still the currency used in ordinary Swedish shops.
